name: Bindi forehead marking

card.summary: A decorative dot worn on the forehead, traditional in South Asia, that draws attention to the centre of the face and finishes an outfit.
card.note: Adhesive in some sticker bindis has caused skin depigmentation and allergic reactions.

quick.overview:
A bindi is a dot worn on the centre of the forehead, traditionally by Hindu, Jain and Buddhist women in the Indian subcontinent. Its name comes from the Sanskrit word bindu, meaning point or drop. It is a cultural and religious mark that also works as facial adornment, adding colour and a focal point between the eyebrows.

Traditional bindis are made from kumkum or sindoor, while modern ones are sticker versions in many colours and shapes. Dermatology literature documents contact reactions to the adhesive and dyes.
quick.how: Bindis are applied as paste with a finger or small disc, or worn as a stick-on sticker, matched to clothing or occasion. Styles vary by region.
quick.risks: Dermatology studies describe contact depigmentation from the adhesive in sticker bindis and allergic reactions to dyes. Cultural commentators have also debated its use as a fashion accessory by people outside the tradition.

lead: A bindi is a dot at the centre of the forehead, worn by Hindus, Jains and Buddhists in the Indian subcontinent, and by Hindus in parts of Southeast Asia.[1] The word comes from Sanskrit bindu, "point" or "dot".[1] It is linked to the ajna chakra, or third eye, and red is associated with honour, love and prosperity, so bindis are often worn by married women.[1]

As adornment, it marks the middle of the face and coordinates with clothing and jewellery. Traditional versions use red or maroon kumkum or sindoor; lac bindis use spangles; modern sticker bindis come in many colours, shapes and sizes.[1] Regional styles include a large crescent in Maharashtra and a large round red dot in Bengal.[1]

Western celebrities including Gwen Stefani, Julia Roberts, Madonna and Selena Gomez have worn bindis, and Selena Gomez's 2013 use drew criticism from Hindu leader Rajan Zed.[1] Dermatology reviews describe skin reactions to sticker bindis.[2][3]

chain: Draws attention to centre of face
angle.text: A bindi adds a focal point to the forehead and coordinates with clothing. In its traditional context it also carries religious and marital meaning.

paras: Indus Valley clay figurines show red marks on the forehead, though their significance is unclear.[1] The Grokipedia summary dates such terracotta finds to around 2500 BCE and also cites later relief carvings such as those at Bharhut (2nd century BCE).[4]

Traditional bindis use kumkum or sindoor, sometimes with sandalwood, turmeric or ash; lac bindis are ornamental; sticker bindis are disposable.[1] In Sindh, kohl dots called tikra serve as an amulet against the evil eye.[1]

Western fashion adoption and criticism of it have been covered in the press; Priyanka Chopra praised Selena Gomez's use as embracing Indian culture, while Rajan Zed said it should not be a fashion accessory.[1] Rapper Lil Uzi Vert debuted a pink diamond bindi in February 2021.[1]

A review of Indian cultural practices says sticker bindis can cause contact leukoderma.[2] A 1990 study of 100 cases found the adhesive contained 80% para-tertiary-butylphenol.[5] Paraphenylenediamine in dyes and adhesives can cause allergic contact dermatitis.[3] Iodine-patch bindis have been used in north-west Maharashtra against iodine deficiency.[1]

Studies concern adverse reactions: contact depigmentation from bindi adhesive in a series of 100 cases,[5] a case report of depigmentation from a sticker bindi, spectacles and a watch strap,[6] and reviews of cultural-practice dermatoses.[2][3]
